crop pest responses to global changes in climate and land management the prevalence of crop insect pests which damage crops and reduce their yield is increasing globally owing to changes in climate and land use posing a threat to food security in this review we synthesize evidence on how tropical temperate migratory and soil crop pests respond to changes in climate land use and agricultural practices in general crop pests are responding to warming with expanded geographic ranges advanced phenological events and increased number of reproductive generations per year increased pest damage under warming is projected to exacerbate yield losses of 46 19 and 31 under 2 c warming for wheat rice and maize respectively pests at midhigh latitudes respond more positively to warming than those in the tropics moderate drought can increase pest damage to crops owing to enhanced feeding on plants as a water source and decreased resilience of plants and natural enemies of pests increased precipitation reduces small pests through washing them away but favours pests in general through buffering thermalhydro stresses land use change such as deforestation and conversion to cropland enhances warming and reduces biodiversity leading to enhanced crop damage agricultural intensification particularly fertilization and irrigation increases the quality and quantity of host plants and buffers pests from environmental extremes favouring proliferation globalization of trade networks increases pest invasions with associated damage exceeding us 423 billion in 2019 future research should examine the mechanisms underlying changes in pest status and develop monitoring and prediction systems to inform management approaches key points climate warming and associated increasing extreme heat events are shifting tropical and temperate pest risks towards higher latitudes and elevations warming and heatwaves are extending the pest damage season delaying pest diapause onset in warm temperate regions but disrupting diapause and weakening cold tolerance in cool temperate regions migratory pests adapt well to global change owing to their high stress tolerances and their migratory behaviour allowing them to track suitable host plants and climate soil pests thrive worldwide as soil buffers them from exposure to extreme climates toxic chemicals and natural predators and pests can locate optimal thermal and moisture conditions through vertical movement within the soil profile agricultural practices such as irrigation and fertilization provide pests with optimal host plant conditions buffer climate stresses and reduce natural biological control through reduced biodiversity whereas btcrop adoption curtails pest population land use changes such as deforestation and cropland expansion proliferate pests by modifying local climates creating favourable conditions for pests and disrupting natural enemies whereas landscape diversification promotes natural pest control key pests impacting crops are aphids for wheat and soybean planthoppers and stem borers for rice and corn borers noctuid caterpillars and locusts for maize warming promotes wheat pest abundance in the spring moves rice pest damage from the subtropics to temperate regions and favours maize and soybean pests yield losses to crop pests and pesticide use are increasing however pests could also decline in the future due to climate extremes genetically modified crops and climatesmart pesticide applications sustainable pest management can be achieved through increasing landscape and biological diversity developing conservation biological control strategies increasing natural enemy biodiversity can help naturally control pest populations and reduce reliance on pesticides

daily reading article for varc practice selfhealing roads a new era in infrastructure as global infrastructure continues to age under the strain of increasing urbanization climate stress and growing traffic loads a revolutionary concept is beginning to take hold selfhealing roads these advanced road materials are designed to autonomously repair cracks and surface damage dramatically extending the lifespan of roads and reducing the need for constant costly maintenance what once sounded like a futuristic idea is now progressing rapidly through research labs and pilot projects across the world the core problem with traditional road surfaces whether made of asphalt or concrete is that they naturally deteriorate over time factors like temperature shifts water infiltration and mechanical stress from vehicles lead to the formation of microcracks left untreated these small imperfections expand into larger structural problems causing potholes surface wear and eventually full road failure conventional repairs are expensive timeconsuming and disruptive selfhealing technology offers a powerful alternative by preventing damage before it becomes visible and critical several advanced approaches are being explored to make this vision a reality one of the most developed techniques involves the incorporation of steel fibers into asphalt mixtures these fibers are conductive and can be heated using electromagnetic induction when cracks form applying induction heat softens the surrounding asphalt allowing it to flow and seal the damage essentially melting the cracks shut this method has already been tested in parts of the netherlands and germany with promising results another innovative strategy includes embedding microcapsules filled with healing agents like rejuvenating bitumen or polymerbased materials into road surfaces when cracks appear these capsules rupture and release their contents which seep into the fissures and restore the materials structural integrity a particularly fascinating development involves the use of bacteriabased concrete researchers have discovered that certain strains of bacteria when added to concrete mixtures in a dormant state can be activated by water that seeps into cracks upon activation these bacteria produce limestone effectively filling the cracks and preventing further damage this method mimics biological healing and holds great promise for bridges tunnels and other concreteheavy infrastructure other systems are also being developed where plantbased oils or synthetic rejuvenators are released from fibers or capsules within the asphalt to refresh the binder material as it ages maintaining elasticity and reducing brittleness countries like germany are already running smallscale trials to evaluate the longterm performance of these materials under real traffic conditions the netherlands has taken the lead in applying inductionbased healing asphalt on actual roadways and is aiming to scale this technology nationwide in the coming decades the united kingdom china south korea and the united states are also investing in various forms of selfhealing infrastructure from bioconcrete to smart asphalt capable of sensing and reporting damage autonomously the benefits of selfhealing roads extend far beyond simple durability they can reduce the frequency and cost of road repairs lower carbon emissions from construction activities and enhance overall road safety by minimizing the time roads are under maintenance with fewer roadworks and longerlasting surfaces both commuters and governments stand to benefit furthermore these technologies align with the goals of smart and sustainable urban planning where infrastructure is expected to be more resilient adaptive and environmentally conscious however challenges remain the upfront cost of selfhealing materials is still significantly higher than traditional materials and largescale implementation demands not only financial investment but also changes in construction standards and public policy questions about performance in extreme climates longterm behavior and recyclability of these new materials are still being researched yet despite these obstacles the momentum behind selfhealing infrastructure is undeniable in the near future roads that heal themselves could become an integral part of our citiesless prone to damage more environmentally friendly and capable of serving society for decades with minimal upkeep as technological advancements continue to push boundaries selfhealing roads may well represent the beginning of a smarter more sustainable era in global infrastructure

why earthing and grounding in middle east infrastructure are important earthing and grounding are fundamental to electrical safety and system stability especially in the middle east where environmental and soil conditions create unique engineering challenges as infrastructure across the region continues to expandranging from oil and gas facilities to highrise buildings and data centersthe role of effective grounding has become increasingly critical in simple terms earthing and grounding provide a controlled path for fault currents lightning energy and electrical surges to safely dissipate into the earth however in middle east environments this process is far from straightforward desert sands commonly found inland exhibit very high soil resistivity when dry while coastal sabkha soils contain high levels of chlorides and sulfates that accelerate corrosion of grounding electrodes carbonate and limestone layers further restrict current dispersion reducing the effectiveness of conventional grounding methods because of these factors poor earthing and grounding can result in dangerous step and touch voltages ineffective lightning protection and instability in surge protection systems in critical facilities such as oil refineries substations airports and commercial towers grounding failure may lead to equipment damage power quality issues and unplanned downtime these risks make grounding not just a compliance requirement but a core element of infrastructure reliability soil mineral composition also plays a major role in longterm grounding performance quartzrich sands are electrically inert sulfates accelerate metal corrosion and chlorides weaken bonding joints seasonal temperature and humidity variations further alter soil resistivity making grounding systems unpredictable if they are not engineered for local conditions modern earthing and grounding solutions in the middle east therefore require an engineered approach this includes integrated grounding grids corrosionresistant electrodes conductive backfills engineered earthing compounds and proper bonding across foundations and structural steel soil resistivity testing and chemical analysis are essential during the design stage to ensure consistent performance over the asset lifecycle as infrastructure becomes more complex and technologydriven reliable earthing and natural ways to control condensation inside shipping containers uk climate top 5 natural ways to control condensation in a shipping container condensation is a common issue in shipping containers especially in the uk climate natural ways to control condensation in a shipping container include using moistureabsorbing materials such as coal cardboard sawdust and rock salt alongside improving natural airflow to stabilise internal humidity these lowcost powerfree methods help keep containers wind and watertight protect stored goods and extend the lifespan of both new and used units what it is natural condensation control explained condensation forms when warm moist air inside a container comes into contact with cold steel surfaces this is a frequent problem in steel storage containers exposed to changing temperatures and damp conditions natural condensation control focuses on absorption where materials pull moisture from the air air movement to reduce humidity buildup and maintaining temperature balance to avoid sudden thermal swings understanding these natural methods helps prevent damp issues and protect valuable stock stored inside containers why condensation matters and the problems it solves if condensation is left unmanaged it can cause a range of problems over time damp or ruined packaging mould and mildew unpleasant odours rust forming on internal steel surfaces and damage to fabrics electronics or furniture are all common outcomes persistent moisture can also reduce the internal lifespan of a container preventing condensation is essential for longterm secure storage and helps reduce maintenance and repair needs coal lump coal coal is a highly effective natural condensation control material due to its porous structure it absorbs moisture slowly from the air helping to reduce overall humidity inside shipping containers used for longterm storage small trays or mesh bags of lump coal can be placed around the container floor ensuring airflow is not blocked the coal should be replaced once it begins to feel noticeably heavy which indicates it has absorbed moisture cardboard sheets or boxes cardboard provides a simple and lowcost way to manage moisture inside steel storage containers sheets or boxes can be placed around the container or between stored items to reduce condensation forming on cold steel panels cardboard works by absorbing excess moisture from the air but it should be replaced once it becomes damp this method is most effective when combined with good natural airflow sawdust sawdust offers strong moisture absorption making it particularly useful in containers storing tools timber or items that naturally release moisture when spread lightly in trays or sacks sawdust absorbs humidity from the surrounding air it should be replaced when it becomes clumpy or saturated this method is especially effective during colder months and is one of the strongest natural options for keeping a wind and watertight container dry through winter rock salt or table salt rock salt and standard table salt act as natural desiccants inside shipping containers salt absorbs moisture from the air and gradually forms brine as humidity levels rise bowls or trays of salt can be placed around the container to help lower internal moisture levels once the salt has fully dissolved it should be replaced this method is lowcost and effective for protecting stored stock during longterm storage natural airflow the most important fix natural airflow is the single most effective way to prevent condensation in a shipping container regularly opening the container doors allows fresh air to circulate and humid air to escape goods should be spaced away from the walls to avoid moisture transfer from cold steel surfaces and overpacking should be avoided raising the container slightly off the ground also helps improve airflow underneath for longterm secure storage natural airflow should always be the foundation of any moisture control strategy final thoughts condensation in shipping containers is a common issue but it can be managed effectively using simple natural methods by combining moisture absorption with proper airflow and sensible storage practices containers can remain dry secure and suitable for longterm use without relying on powered systems or chemical treatments happy to answer questions or share further experience if anyone is dealing with condensation problems in their container

situation before novdec 2025 ambiguity there was no single uniform definition of the aravali hills across the four states delhi haryana rajasthan gujarat varied criteria states used different methods to identify these areas revenue records some areas were defined based on terms like gair mumkin pahad uncultivable hill in land records notifications the 1992 aravali notification restricted activities in specific districts like gurgaon and alwar but did not clearly define the geological boundaries of a hill visualdictionary definitions courts often had to rely on dictionary definitions of a hill or forest leading to disputes over whether a lowlying ridge or a scrub forest qualified for protection result this lack of clarity created grey areas where illegal mining often thrived a uniform elevationbased definition proposed by the ministry of environment forest and climate change moefcc aravali hill any landform in the aravali districts that has an elevation of 100 meters or relationship contribution and truthaligned action the shadow conaf emerges when these needs are chronically unmet threatened or destabilized politics becomes a surrogate environment where those unmet chutillu cycloneresistant housing innovation from indias coastal communities introduction the eastern coastline of india has long been vulnerable to devastating tropical cyclones that emerge from the bay of bengal among the various indigenous responses to this persistent threat the chutillu housing system stands out as a remarkable example of vernacular architecture adapted to extreme weather conditions originating from the coastal regions of andhra pradesh and parts of tamil nadu chutillu houses represent centuries of accumulated wisdom in building techniques that can withstand the fury of cyclonic winds and storm surges while remaining affordable and accessible to rural communities the name chutillu itself derives from local terminology with variations in spelling and pronunciation across different regions these structures embody the principle that effective disasterresistant architecture need not be technologically complex or financially prohibitive instead they demonstrate how careful attention to design principles material selection and construction methods can create resilient housing solutions that serve communities generation after generation historical context and geographic distribution chutillu houses emerged in response to the cycloneprone geography of indias southeastern coast the bay of bengal generates some of the worlds most intense tropical cyclones and the flat coastal plains of states like andhra pradesh offer little natural protection from these storms historical records document numerous devastating cyclones that have struck this region over centuries each leaving lessons that were gradually incorporated into local building practices the concentration of chutillustyle construction is particularly notable in coastal districts where fishing communities and agricultural workers required housing that could endure seasonal cyclones without requiring complete reconstruction after each storm unlike more permanent brick and concrete structures that were economically out of reach for many rural families or simple thatch shelters that offered inadequate protection chutillu houses occupied a middle groundproviding substantial cyclone resistance while remaining within the economic means of ordinary villagers fundamental design principles the genius of chutillu architecture lies in its adherence to several key design principles that collectively enhance cyclone resistance the first and most important principle is the creation of a low profile chutillu houses are typically singlestory structures with relatively low roof heights compared to conventional houses this reduced height minimizes the surface area exposed to highvelocity winds thereby reducing the wind load on the structure the lower center of gravity also contributes to overall stability during storms aerodynamic considerations play a crucial role in the design the roofs of chutillu houses are typically designed with slopes that allow wind to flow over the structure rather than creating uplift forces that could tear the roof away the shape is often compared to an overturned boat with smooth curves that deflect wind rather than resisting it headon this principle of working with natural forces rather than against them represents a sophisticated understanding of fluid dynamics developed through observation and experimentation over generations the structural system of chutillu houses emphasizes flexibility over rigidity unlike modern reinforced concrete structures that derive their strength from rigid frames chutillu houses incorporate elements that can flex and move with the wind to some degree without failing this flexibility allows the structure to absorb and dissipate wind energy rather than resisting it until a catastrophic failure point is reached timber frames and bamboo elements are connected in ways that permit slight movement while maintaining overall structural integrity materials and construction techniques traditional chutillu houses utilize locally available materials that possess inherent properties suitable for cyclone resistance the primary structural frame often consists of timber posts and beams selected for their strengthtoweight ratio the use of lighter materials throughout the structure means that even if components fail during a severe storm they pose less danger to occupants than heavy materials like concrete or masonry would bamboo features prominently in many chutillu constructions particularly for secondary structural elements and wall panels the natural flexibility and tensile strength of bamboo make it ideal for cycloneresistant construction bamboo elements can bend significantly under wind pressure without snapping and the materials light weight reduces the overall load on the foundation various species of bamboo are selected based on their specific properties with larger diameter culms used for primary supports and smaller ones for infill and roofing elements the walls of chutillu houses are often constructed using wattleanddaub techniques or woven bamboo mats plastered with a mixture of mud cow dung and sometimes lime these wall systems are semipermeable allowing some air flow through the structure which helps equalize pressure during cyclones and prevents the dangerous buildup of internal pressure that can cause roofs to explode outward the walls are designed to be the weakest link in the structural systemthey may fail during extreme events but their failure allows pressure relief without causing total structural collapse roofing materials traditionally include thatch made from palmyra palm leaves coconut fronds or dried grasses though in modern iterations corrugated metal sheets or clay tiles may be used the attachment of roofing material is critical to cyclone resistance traditional methods involve tying thatch bundles to the roof frame using coir rope or natural fibers in intricate patterns that distribute loads evenly and prevent individual bundles from being stripped away by wind when metal roofing is used special attention must be paid to fastening methods as improperly secured metal sheets become dangerous projectiles in cyclonic winds foundation and anchoring systems the foundation system of chutillu houses reflects an understanding of soil mechanics and the forces exerted during cyclones in sandy coastal soils shallow foundations can be prone to undermining by storm surge and erosion traditional chutillu foundations often extend deeper than might seem necessary for a light wooden structure providing anchorage against uplift forces and lateral loads foundation posts are sometimes set in stonefilled pits and surrounded with rammed earth or a mixture of lime and earth that hardens over time in some variations the posts are charred at their base before burial a technique that protects against rot and termite damage while increasing the posts lifespan the depth and preparation of these foundation elements are critical to the structures ability to remain anchored during storm conditions some chutillu designs incorporate groundlevel or slightly elevated floor platforms rather than building directly on the earth these raised platforms serve multiple purposes they provide protection from minor flooding allow air circulation beneath the structure which helps prevent moisturerelated deterioration and create a more stable base for the superstructure the elevation is typically modestjust enough to achieve these functional benefits without significantly raising the structures profile or center of gravity innovations in traditional design within the traditional chutillu framework various regional innovations have emerged over time some coastal communities developed techniques for creating more secure door and window shutters that could be quickly fastened before a storm preventing wind and rain from entering the structure these shutters often feature diagonal bracing patterns that provide strength while using minimal material the arrangement of interior spaces in chutillu houses often reflects disaster preparedness considerations storage areas for food water and essential supplies are sometimes built into the structure itself ensuring that families can shelter in place during and immediately after a cyclone some designs include reinforced interior rooms or cores where families can take refuge if the outer envelope of the house is breached ventilation systems represent another area of innovation while maintaining structural integrity traditional builders developed various methods for allowing air circulation even when the house is shuttered for a storm these might include protected ventilation openings near the roof peak or carefully positioned gaps in wall construction that provide airflow without compromising strength modern adaptations and improvements contemporary architects and engineers have studied chutillu houses to
